aiPrompts.task: Niche-specific content strategy generator
aiPrompts.prompt:
Build a 90-day content strategy for a B2B client.

Client niche: [their industry]
Target buyer persona: [their ICP]
Top 5 competitor blogs: [URLs]
Their goal: [SEO traffic / thought leadership / lead gen / demand capture]
Their voice: [formal / casual / contrarian / educational]

Output:

PILLAR TOPICS (3-5):
Each one a long-tail-keyword anchor that supports 8-12 cluster posts.

PILLAR CONTENT (3 anchor pieces, 2500-3500 words each):
- Title + working subhed
- H2 outline (8-10 sections)
- Internal link plan (which cluster posts feed in)
- CTA / conversion path

CLUSTER POSTS (24, organized by pillar):
- Title (with target keyword + search volume estimate)
- Format type (how-to / comparison / listicle / deep-dive / case study)
- Word count target
- Primary keyword + 2 supporting LSI keywords
- Distribution plan (newsletter, LinkedIn, niche communities)

DISTRIBUTION CADENCE:
2 posts/week schedule with promotion checklist per post.

KPIs to track at 30/60/90 days.

aiPrompts.task: Long-form blog post (1500-2500 words, SEO-optimized)
aiPrompts.prompt:
Write a 2000-word blog post for [client] in [niche].

Title: [paste exact target title]
Primary keyword: [keyword + search volume + intent]
Supporting keywords: [3-5 LSI / related terms]
Target buyer persona: [ICP]
Existing top-3 SERP competitors: [paste URLs to differentiate from]
Brand voice: [formal/casual/contrarian — paste 2-3 sample sentences]

Structure:
- H1 (use exact title)
- Hook intro (180-220 words, problem-aware → benefit tease)
- 6-8 H2 sections (each 200-350 words with H3 subsections where helpful)
- Visual cue suggestions (tables, charts, screenshots)
- Internal link suggestions to 3-5 related cluster posts
- CTA section (no hard sell — soft offer)

Quality bar:
- Every claim has a source or qualifier
- Reads like a senior practitioner wrote it, not AI
- Hooks every 200 words to prevent bounce
- Avoids AI tells (delve, leverage, treasure trove, in conclusion, navigate the landscape)

Output the full post + meta description (150-160 chars) + 5 internal link anchor suggestions.

resources.whatItTakes: You need to be able to write clearly, meet deadlines without being chased, and handle the awkward silence after you send a pitch that gets ignored. SEO basics matter more than most beginners expect: knowing how to structure an article around a keyword, use headers well, and write a meta description that doesn't sound robotic will separate you from the pile fast. You don't need a journalism degree or a portfolio of 50 pieces. You need 3 solid samples, a clear niche, and the discipline to show up when the work feels slow.
resources.whereTheyFail: Most beginners write generalist pitches — 'I can write about anything!' — and wonder why no one bites. Clients hiring freelancers want someone who already speaks their industry's language. The second failure point is underpricing to get started and then getting stuck there, afraid to raise rates on clients who've gotten comfortable with the low number. The third is treating every piece of feedback as an attack rather than a brief. Writers who last learn to separate their ego from their drafts early.
resources.theDip: Weeks three through eight are where most people quietly stop. You've sent pitches, maybe gotten one or two nibbles, possibly done a paid test piece — and then silence. The inbox is empty, the bank account hasn't moved, and it's easy to conclude this doesn't work. It does work, but the pipeline takes time to fill. The writers who get through the dip are the ones who keep sending five pitches a week even when it feels pointless, who treat rejection as a numbers game, and who use the slow weeks to sharpen their samples instead of second-guessing the whole plan.

aiPrompts.task: Create an SEO-optimized blog post outline for a client
aiPrompts.prompt:
I'm writing a blog post for a client in the [INDUSTRY] space. The target keyword is '[PRIMARY KEYWORD]' with a monthly search volume of roughly [VOLUME]. The reader is [DESCRIBE READER — e.g., 'a small business owner who wants to improve their Google ranking but has no technical background'].

Give me:
1. An H1 title that includes the primary keyword naturally and would make someone click
2. A meta description under 155 characters
3. A full outline with H2s and H2s, including:
 - An intro hook (problem or surprising stat)

 - A FAQ section with 3 questions real people search

aiPrompts.task: Turn a rough draft into a polished, client-ready article
aiPrompts.prompt:
I've written a rough draft of a [WORD COUNT]-word blog post on the topic '[TOPIC]' for a client in the [INDUSTRY] industry. The target audience is [READER DESCRIPTION]. The primary keyword is '[KEYWORD]'.

Here is my draft:
[PASTE DRAFT HERE]

Please:
1. Improve sentence flow and readability — aim for a Flesch-Kincaid reading ease score of 60-70 (clear, not dumbed down)
2. Strengthen the opening hook — the first 2 sentences must make the reader want to keep going
3. Check that the primary keyword appears in: the first 100 words, at least 2 H2s, and naturally 3-5 more times in the body
4. Flag any claims that need a source or citation with [NEEDS SOURCE]
5. Tighten any paragraph longer than 5 lines
6. Suggest a stronger CTA for the conclusion

Do NOT change my voice or add fluff. Return the revised draft with a short bullet summary of changes made.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing for any client in any niche with no specialization
commonMistakes.why: Generalist writers compete on price alone. When you claim to write 'anything,' clients have no reason to choose you over the cheapest option on Fiverr. You also spend enormous time learning new industries from scratch on every project, which kills your effective hourly rate.
commonMistakes.prevention: Pick 1-2 niches where you already have knowledge or genuine curiosity — SaaS, personal finance, health, legal, etc.

commonMistakes.mistake: Delivering work with no contract or scope agreement
commonMistakes.why: Scope creep is the silent income killer in freelance writing. A client who asked for '1 blog post' suddenly wants 3 revisions, a rewrite for a different audience, and a social media caption version — all for the original price. Without a contract, you have no standing to say no.
commonMistakes.prevention: Use a simple one-page contract (Bonsai or HelloSign templates work fine) that defines: word count, number of revision rounds, turnaround time, and what constitutes a new request.

commonMistakes.mistake: Setting rates based on what you think clients will pay rather than your time cost
commonMistakes.why: New writers chronically underprice. That's below minimum wage in most states and unsustainable within weeks.
commonMistakes.prevention: Calculate your minimum viable hourly rate first (monthly expenses ÷ available hours), then price per project based on estimated hours × target rate.

commonMistakes.why: Freelance writing income feels stable until a single client cuts their content budget, hires in-house, or disappears without warning.
commonMistakes.prevention: Treat client concentration like a business risk. Actively pursue new clients even when you're fully booked. Build a small pipeline of 3-5 active clients at all times.

commonMistakes.mistake: Skipping the editing pass and delivering first-draft quality work
commonMistakes.why: Clients don't see your research time or how fast you write — they only see the final document. Typos, weak transitions, and thin arguments signal that you don't care about their brand. One sloppy deliverable can end a client relationship and damage your referral reputation.
commonMistakes.prevention: Build a mandatory self-edit step into every project: finish the draft, step away for at least 30 minutes, then read it aloud before submitting. Use Grammarly or Hemingway Editor as a second pass. Never submit work you wouldn't be proud to show as a portfolio sample.

decisionTrees.question: What niche should I write in?

options.choice: Write in a niche tied to your professional background
options.pickIf: You have 1+ years of work experience in any industry — healthcare, finance, tech, legal, real estate, marketing, etc.
options.nextStep: Lean into that expertise immediately. A former nurse writing health content or a former software developer writing SaaS content commands premium rates because they understand the audience and don't need 3 hours of research per article.

options.choice: Write in a niche you're genuinely curious about and willing to study
options.pickIf: You're a career changer with no obvious professional niche, but you have a strong personal interest in a specific area
options.nextStep: Spend 2-4 weeks reading industry publications, newsletters, and top blogs in that niche. Write 2-3 spec pieces demonstrating your understanding before pitching. Clients can tell the difference between a curious learner and someone faking expertise.

options.choice: Stay general until a niche emerges naturally
options.pickIf: You genuinely have no preference yet and want to try different types of work before committing
options.nextStep: Take 3-5 varied projects in your first 2 months, then look at which ones you produced fastest, enjoyed most, and got the best client feedback on. That intersection is your niche signal.

resources.whatItTakes: Podcasting rewards people who can show up consistently and talk clearly about something they genuinely care about. You don't need a studio voice or expensive gear — a decent USB mic and a quiet room will do. What you do need is the patience to publish episodes before anyone is listening, the discipline to edit audio without losing your mind, and enough curiosity about your topic to keep going past episode 20 when downloads are still small. This is a slow-build game. Monetization usually comes through sponsorships, listener support, or selling your own products to a small but loyal audience — not from ad revenue on a few hundred downloads. If you want to talk, teach, or tell stories, and you're willing to treat it like a craft rather than a lottery ticket, podcasting can work.
resources.whereTheyFail: Most podcasters quit between episodes 10 and 20. That's when the novelty has worn off, the download numbers are still modest, and the editing feels like a chore. People also fail by chasing broad topics — 'entrepreneurship' or 'wellness' — instead of going narrow enough to matter to a specific audience. Another common trap: spending weeks perfecting audio quality and show art before publishing a single episode. The show doesn't get better in isolation. It gets better by doing it in public and responding to what listeners actually respond to.
resources.theDip: Around weeks six through twelve, you'll be publishing regularly, getting decent feedback from a handful of listeners, and still making exactly zero dollars. This is the dip. The audience isn't big enough for sponsors to care, and it's too early to know if your format is working. The temptation here is to either pivot the whole show or give up entirely. What actually works is narrowing your niche further, reaching out personally to the small audience you do have, and being honest with yourself about whether you're improving episode to episode. The dip lifts — but only if you keep publishing.

aiPrompts.task: Generate a full episode outline from a single topic idea

I host a podcast about [YOUR NICHE, e.g. 'personal finance for freelancers']. My target listener is [DESCRIBE LISTENER, e.g. 'a 28-35 year old freelance designer who earns $50k-$80k and struggles with inconsistent income'].

Topic for this episode: [YOUR TOPIC IDEA]

Please create a full episode outline with:
1. A compelling episode title (not clickbait, just clear and specific)
2. A one-sentence episode premise that explains exactly what the listener will learn
3. A cold open hook (first 60 seconds — what problem or question pulls them in)
4. 3-5 main segments with talking points under each (bullet form, not full scripts)
5. A natural transition between each segment
6. A specific, actionable takeaway the listener can do TODAY
7. A call-to-action for the outro (what do I want them to do next?)

Keep the tone [DESCRIBE YOUR TONE, e.g. 'conversational, slightly nerdy, no fluff']. Target episode length is [YOUR TARGET LENGTH, e.g. '25-35 minutes'] so calibrate the depth accordingly.

aiPrompts.task: Write show notes, SEO description, and social captions for one episode
aiPrompts.prompt:
Here is the transcript (or rough summary) of my latest podcast episode:

[PASTE TRANSCRIPT OR BULLET SUMMARY HERE]

My podcast is called [SHOW NAME] and it's about [ONE SENTENCE DESCRIPTION]. My target listener is [LISTENER DESCRIPTION].

Please write:
1. SHOW NOTES (250-400 words): Conversational summary of what we covered, written for someone who hasn't listened yet. Include a 'What you'll learn' bullet list of 3-5 specific points. End with a natural CTA.
2. SEO DESCRIPTION (150 words max): Optimized for the search phrase '[YOUR TARGET KEYWORD]'. Should read naturally, not keyword-stuffed.
3. INSTAGRAM CAPTION: 150-200 words, starts with a hook line, includes 3-5 relevant hashtags at the end.
4. TWITTER/X THREAD: 4-6 tweets, first tweet is a hook, middle tweets share one insight each, final tweet links to the episode.
5. ONE LINKEDIN POST: 200-250 words, professional but personal tone, no hashtag spam (max 3 hashtags).

Do not use the phrase 'In this episode' to start the show notes. Make every piece feel like it was written by a human who actually listened.

I need to write a cold outreach email for my podcast. Here are the details:

MY PODCAST:
- Name: [SHOW NAME]
- Niche: [NICHE]
- Episode count: [NUMBER]
- Average downloads per episode: [NUMBER]
- Audience: [DESCRIBE IN ONE SENTENCE]

WHO I'M REACHING OUT TO: [GUEST NAME / COMPANY NAME]
WHY THEM SPECIFICALLY: [ONE SPECIFIC REASON — a book they wrote, a company they run, a post they made]
WHAT I WANT: [Guest appearance / Sponsorship / Cross-promotion]

Please write:
1. A subject line (under 8 words, no exclamation marks)
2. An email body (under 180 words) that:
 - Opens with the specific reason I'm reaching out to THEM (not a generic compliment)
 - Explains what's in it for them in one sentence
 - Gives my podcast credibility without bragging (use the numbers above)

aiPrompts.task: Validate a new podcast niche before you record a single episode
aiPrompts.prompt:
I'm considering starting a podcast in this niche: [DESCRIBE YOUR NICHE IDEA IN 2-3 SENTENCES, including who the listener is and what problem it solves].

Please help me validate this before I invest time:

1. COMPETITION AUDIT: What types of shows likely already exist in this space? What gaps might exist (underserved sub-niches, underserved audience segments, missing formats)?

2. MONETIZATION REALITY CHECK: What are the realistic monetization paths for a show in this niche? Which paths require scale (large audience) vs. which work at small audience sizes (under 1,000 downloads/episode)?

3. CONTENT LONGEVITY: Is this niche evergreen, trend-dependent, or seasonal? What does that mean for long-term sustainability?

4. AUDIENCE SPECIFICITY TEST: Is my target listener specific enough? If not, suggest 2-3 ways to narrow it down.

5. RED FLAGS: What are the honest reasons this niche might be hard to monetize or grow?

Be direct. I'd rather hear the hard truth now than after recording 20 episodes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Buying expensive equipment before validating the show concept
commonMistakes.why: Most new podcasters quit before episode 10. Equipment doesn't make a bad concept good.
commonMistakes.prevention: Only upgrade once you've hit 20 episodes and confirmed you're staying.

commonMistakes.mistake: Targeting a niche that's too broad to attract loyal listeners or sponsors
commonMistakes.why: 'Entrepreneurship' or 'health and wellness' are categories, not niches. Sponsors pay for specific audiences (e.g. 'female founders in e-commerce'), not general ones. Broad shows also struggle to grow because they don't give listeners a clear reason to subscribe over the thousands of other shows in the same space.
commonMistakes.prevention: Use the 'who, what, and why now' test: Who exactly is your listener (be specific about their situation), what specific problem do you solve, and why is this the moment they need your show? If you can't answer all three in one sentence, narrow further.

commonMistakes.mistake: Chasing download numbers instead of building a monetizable audience
commonMistakes.why: Download count is a vanity metric. A show with 300 highly engaged listeners in a specific professional niche can earn more from sponsorships or a paid community than a general show with 5,000 passive listeners. Operators optimize for the wrong number and burn out before they find the real revenue lever.
commonMistakes.prevention: From episode one, build an email list. Ask listeners to join a newsletter or community. Track email subscribers and engagement rates alongside downloads. These are the numbers sponsors and course buyers actually care about.

commonMistakes.mistake: Inconsistent publishing schedule
commonMistakes.why: Podcast algorithms on Spotify and Apple reward consistency. More importantly, listeners build habits. If you publish every Tuesday for 6 weeks then disappear for 3 weeks, you lose the habit loop. Subscriber churn from inconsistency is nearly impossible to recover from in the first 6 months.
commonMistakes.prevention: Batch record 3-4 episodes before you launch publicly. Commit to a schedule you can keep on your worst week — biweekly is better than weekly-when-you-can. Use a content calendar and record buffer episodes during good weeks.

commonMistakes.mistake: Waiting until you have a large audience to monetize
commonMistakes.why: Most podcasters think they need 10,000 downloads per episode to earn money. This is false. Affiliate marketing, consulting leads, digital products, and niche sponsorships are all viable at 200-500 downloads per episode if your audience is specific and engaged. Waiting means leaving real money on the table for 12-18 months.
commonMistakes.prevention: Identify your monetization path before you record episode one. If it's consulting leads, mention your services from episode 1. If it's affiliate marketing, join programs in your niche immediately. Don't wait for 'enough' listeners — start small and iterate.

resources.whatItTakes: You're essentially a translator between what AI tools can do and what regular people wish they could get out of them. That means you need to spend real time inside ChatGPT, Midjourney, Claude, and whatever else is gaining traction — not just dabbling, but systematically testing what works and documenting why. The people who build sustainable prompt shops aren't the most technical; they're the most organized and the most honest about what their prompts actually produce. You'll write clear copy, build a simple SEO-friendly storefront on Gumroad or Etsy, and gradually build a small audience who trusts your curation. This is a volume-and-trust game: a handful of prompts won't cut it, and a large catalogue with sloppy results won't either. Expect to publish 20–40 tested, well-documented prompts before the shop starts feeling real.
resources.whereTheyFail: Most people list five or ten prompts, get no sales in the first two weeks, and decide the market is saturated. It's not saturated — it's just that their shop has no traffic, no trust signals, and no clear buyer in mind. The second failure mode is writing prompts that look good in a screenshot but fall apart when a real user tries them in a slightly different context. Buyers leave bad reviews, refund requests pile up, and confidence crumbles. A third trap: chasing every new AI tool the moment it drops instead of going deep on one niche. Depth beats breadth here, especially early.
resources.theDip: Weeks four through ten are brutal. You've built the shop, posted on Reddit or Twitter once or twice, and sales are either zero or a trickle. The prompts feel obvious to you now, so you start wondering if anyone actually needs them. This is the moment most people either abandon the shop or pivot randomly to a completely different niche, which resets the clock. The people who get through it pick one specific audience — say, real estate agents using ChatGPT, or indie game developers using Midjourney — and go all-in on serving that one group well before expanding. The dip is a focus problem disguised as a sales problem.

- Different buyer personas (e.g., targeting a VP vs. a founder vs. a procurement manager)

1. Open with a specific, relatable problem the reader has (not a generic intro)
2. Briefly explain why most people's DIY prompts underperform

4. Include a natural CTA toward the end pointing to my prompt pack store (URL: [YOUR URL]) — don't make it salesy, just helpful

commonMistakes.mistake: Building packs nobody searched for
commonMistakes.why: Most beginners pick topics they personally find interesting (e.g., 'prompts for writing poetry') instead of topics buyers are actively searching for. Low-demand niches produce zero sales regardless of quality.
commonMistakes.prevention: Before building any pack, spend 30 minutes checking search volume on Ubersuggest or Google Keyword Planner for '[niche] ChatGPT prompts'. Also check PromptBase's bestseller list and Gumroad's discover page to see what's already selling.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pricing too low out of fear
commonMistakes.why: At that price you need hundreds of sales to earn meaningful income. It also undercuts your own perceived value.
commonMistakes.prevention: Test a higher price first — you can always discount, but it's hard to raise prices on a listing with reviews.

commonMistakes.mistake: Selling generic prompts that buyers could Google for free
commonMistakes.why: Prompts like 'write me a blog post about X' have no scarcity value. Buyers will leave a bad review or request a refund when they realize the prompts aren't meaningfully better than what they already knew.
commonMistakes.prevention: Every prompt in your pack should include specificity that takes real effort to craft: role-setting, output format instructions, tone constraints, chain-of-thought triggers, or industry-specific context. Test every prompt yourself before publishing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Relying on a single platform with no owned audience
commonMistakes.why: Gumroad has had policy and fee changes. If your entire revenue depends on one platform's algorithm, you're one policy update away from zero.
commonMistakes.prevention: From day one, collect email addresses. Offer a free 3-prompt sampler in exchange for an email signup. Build a simple newsletter even if it's just monthly. Your email list is the only asset you fully own.

commonMistakes.mistake: Not updating prompts when AI models change
commonMistakes.why: A prompt optimized for GPT-3.5 may produce noticeably worse results on GPT-4o or Claude 3.5. Buyers who purchase later get a worse experience than early buyers, leading to refunds and bad reviews.
commonMistakes.prevention: Set a quarterly reminder to re-test your top 5 selling packs on the current model versions. Update the listing description to note which model version was tested. This also gives you a reason to email your list ('Updated for GPT-4o').

aiPrompts.task: Write a full YouTube script optimized for watch time and AI voiceover
aiPrompts.prompt:
Write a full YouTube script for a faceless channel on this topic: [INSERT VIDEO TITLE AND KEYWORD].

Channel niche: [your niche]
Target video length: 8-10 minutes (approximately 1,200-1,500 words spoken)
Voiceover style: [calm and authoritative / energetic and conversational / storytelling narrator — pick one]

Script requirements:
1. Open with a pattern-interrupt hook in the first 15 seconds — state the problem or surprising fact, do NOT start with 'In this video'
2. Include a retention loop at the 30-second mark ('stick around because...')
3. Use short sentences (max 20 words each) — this will be read by an AI voice, so no complex clauses
4. Add [PAUSE] markers where the narrator should breathe
5. Add [B-ROLL: description] tags every 30-45 seconds so I know what footage to layer over the voiceover
6. Include 2-3 pattern interrupts mid-video (a surprising stat, a question to the viewer, a scene change cue)
7. End with a soft CTA to subscribe and watch a related video — no hard sell
8. Naturally include the keyword '[INSERT KEYWORD]' in the first 100 words and 3-4 more times throughout

Format: Write the script in plain paragraphs with [PAUSE], [B-ROLL], and [CUT TO] markers inline. Do not include timestamps.

2. A YouTube description (300-400 words) that:

 - Summarizes the video value in plain language

 - Has a timestamps section (use placeholder times like 0:00, 1:30, 3:45 — I'll fill in real ones)
 - Ends with a subscribe CTA and links section placeholder

3. A tag list of 15-20 tags: mix of exact-match keywords, broad topic tags, and long-tail variations. Format as comma-separated.

4. A suggested thumbnail text overlay (5 words max, high contrast, what the text should say to drive clicks).

commonMistakes.mistake: Picking a niche based on passion instead of monetization potential
commonMistakes.prevention: Before filming a single video, look up the estimated RPM for your niche using channels like Niche Pursuits or Income School on YouTube, or ask in creator forums. Finance, business, software, and health are historically strong.

commonMistakes.mistake: Publishing inconsistently after the first month
commonMistakes.why: YouTube's algorithm rewards channels that publish on a predictable schedule. New channels that post 8 videos then go quiet for 3 weeks see their impressions crater. The algorithm stops serving your content because it can't predict your next upload.
commonMistakes.prevention: Batch-produce content. Before you publish video 1, have videos 2, 3, and 4 fully edited and ready. Set a realistic cadence (1-2 videos/week) you can sustain with your actual life, not your optimistic life. Use a content calendar with hard deadlines.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using AI voiceover without editing for naturalness
commonMistakes.why: Raw AI voiceover (ElevenLabs, Murf, etc.) sounds robotic at default settings. Viewers notice within 20 seconds and click away. A high average view duration requires a voice that sounds human.
commonMistakes.prevention: Adjust AI voice speed, pitch, and pause settings. Add subtle background music at -20db to mask robotic artifacts. Read your script aloud yourself first — rewrite any sentence that sounds unnatural when spoken. Test 3-4 voice options before committing to one for your channel.

commonMistakes.mistake: Applying for YouTube Partner Program too early or with the wrong content
commonMistakes.why: YouTube manually reviews channels at monetization application. Channels with AI-generated content that is clearly low-effort, repetitive, or 'made for kids' get rejected or demonetized immediately. Some operators also apply before they have a clear niche identity, which raises flags.
commonMistakes.prevention: Wait until you have 20+ videos with genuine viewer value — not just filler. Make sure your content is clearly for adults (if targeting adult niches), has real informational value, and doesn't reuse the same script structure 20 times. Read YouTube's monetization policies before applying.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring thumbnails and treating them as an afterthought
commonMistakes.why: On YouTube, your thumbnail IS your ad.
commonMistakes.prevention: Spend at least 20-30 minutes on every thumbnail. Study the top 5 performing thumbnails in your niche — what colors, text size, facial expressions (or lack thereof) do they use? For faceless channels, use bold text, high-contrast backgrounds, and a single clear visual. Test A/B thumbnails once you hit 1,000 subscribers.

commonMistakes.mistake: Picking a niche that's interesting to you but has no monetization path
commonMistakes.why: A newsletter about something you love (e.g. 'vintage fountain pens') can grow a loyal audience that will never pay for ads or subscriptions because there's no commercial ecosystem around it. Passion alone doesn't pay the bills.
commonMistakes.prevention: Before you write issue one, identify at least three companies that already advertise to this audience (check Sponsorgap.com or look at similar newsletters' ad slots). If you can't find three, the niche is likely too small or too non-commercial to monetize.

commonMistakes.mistake: Publishing inconsistently in the first 90 days
commonMistakes.why: Email is a habit. Readers expect you on a specific day. Missing even two issues in the first 90 days trains your audience that you're unreliable, kills open rates, and stalls word-of-mouth growth — which is your cheapest acquisition channel early on.
commonMistakes.prevention: Write and schedule the first four issues before you launch. Set a non-negotiable publish day. If life gets in the way, send a shorter issue — even 200 words — rather than skip. Use AI to draft faster when you're short on time.

commonMistakes.mistake: Monetizing too early with ads before building engagement
commonMistakes.why: Running sponsor ads to a list under 500 people (or with open rates below 30%) looks desperate to sponsors and annoys early readers who signed up for content, not ads. You'll get low-ball offers or none at all, and risk early unsubscribes.
commonMistakes.prevention: Wait until you have 500+ subscribers and a 35%+ open rate before pitching sponsors. Use that early period to test paid subscriptions via a 'founding member' offer to your most engaged readers instead — it's more honest and often more profitable at small scale.

commonMistakes.mistake: Relying entirely on AI-written content without adding personal perspective
commonMistakes.why: AI can research and draft, but it produces generic output that sounds like every other newsletter. Readers subscribe to a person, not a content aggregator. If your newsletter could have been written by anyone, it will be replaced by anyone — including free AI tools your readers already have.
commonMistakes.prevention: The rule: AI drafts, you edit and inject. Every issue needs at least one original opinion, personal story, or contrarian take that only you could write. This is your moat. It takes 15-20 extra minutes and is the difference between a newsletter people forward and one they delete.

commonMistakes.mistake: Building on a free platform without owning your subscriber list
commonMistakes.why: Platforms like LinkedIn Newsletter or Substack own the relationship with your readers. If they change their algorithm, terms, or shut down your account, you lose everything. This has happened repeatedly and will keep happening.
commonMistakes.prevention: Always export your subscriber list monthly as a CSV backup regardless of platform. Ideally, use an ESP (email service provider) where you own the list outright — Beehiiv, Kit (formerly ConvertKit), or Mailchimp. Substack is fine to start but migrate before you have 2,000+ subscribers.

decisionTrees.question: My open rates are dropping. What do I do?

options.nextStep: Export subscribers who haven't opened in 90 days. Send a re-engagement email ('Should I keep sending you this?'). Remove anyone who doesn't respond or click within 2 weeks. A smaller, engaged list is worth more than a large cold one — to you and to sponsors.

options.pickIf: Open rate dropped suddenly (last 2-4 issues) but your list is relatively new and hasn't been cleaned before
options.nextStep: A/B test subject lines using your ESP's built-in feature. Try three formats: curiosity gap, direct benefit, and ultra-short (under 30 characters). Run tests for 4 consecutive issues and compare. Subject line is the single highest-leverage variable for open rate.

options.choice: Audit your content quality and consistency
options.pickIf: Open rates have been declining gradually over 3+ months and you've been inconsistent with publish schedule or content quality
options.nextStep: Survey your most engaged subscribers (reply to your next issue asking one question: 'What would make this newsletter more valuable to you?'). Read the last 8 issues critically. Identify where you got lazy or generic. Fix the content before worrying about subject lines.

decisionTrees.question: Should I niche down further or broaden my topic to grow faster?

options.pickIf: You're under 1,000 subscribers, growth is slow, and your current topic feels competitive or hard to differentiate
options.nextStep: Identify the single most engaged segment of your current audience (look at who replies, who clicks most). Build the next 8 issues specifically for that person. Narrow positioning makes word-of-mouth referrals much easier — readers know exactly who to forward it to.

options.pickIf: You've exhausted your core topic's content depth, have 1,500+ subscribers, and see consistent demand for adjacent topics in reader replies
options.nextStep: Introduce adjacent content gradually — one new section or format per month. Watch click rates on new content closely. Only keep what readers engage with. Don't rebrand; just expand scope incrementally.

options.pickIf: You're under 6 months in, growing steadily (even slowly), and have not yet tried the obvious growth channels (cross-promotions, referral program, social posting of issue excerpts)
options.nextStep: Before changing your content strategy, try the growth tactics you haven't tried yet. Most newsletters plateau because of distribution problems, not content problems. Set up a referral program and do 3 newsletter cross-promotions before reconsidering your niche.

resources.whatItTakes: You're running a production shop, not just pressing buttons in an AI tool. Clients hire you because they don't have time to learn HeyGen or figure out what makes a 60-second explainer actually convert. That means you need a real opinion on script structure, pacing, and what a finished video should accomplish — not just technical fluency. The AI handles rendering; you handle judgment. resources.whereTheyFail: Most people fail at the sales step, not the production step. They get good at Runway and Synthesia, build a demo reel, and then wait for clients to find them. Nobody comes. resources.theDip: Weeks four through ten are the hard stretch. You've done a few free or cheap videos, you know the tools, but you haven't landed a real paying client yet. Your outreach feels like shouting into a void. The AI tools keep updating and you feel like you're always catching up. This is where most people quietly close the Notion doc and go back to scrolling. The people who get through it are doing two things: they're sending ten to fifteen personalized outreach messages a week (not blasting), and they're iterating their portfolio based on the feedback they're actually getting, not the portfolio they wish they had.

You are an expert video scriptwriter specializing in short-form business explainer videos. Write a 60-second video script (approximately 150 words of spoken dialogue) for the following:

Business name: [CLIENT BUSINESS NAME]
Product/service: [WHAT THEY SELL]
Target audience: [WHO BUYS FROM THEM]

My agency produces: explainer videos, video ads, and training videos using AI tools (HeyGen, Synthesia, Runway). Turnaround is 3-5 business days. Prices start at $[YOUR STARTING PRICE].

aiPrompts.task: Audit a finished AI video for quality issues before client delivery
aiPrompts.prompt:
I just finished producing an AI-generated video for a client and need to do a quality check before delivery. Act as a harsh but fair video production reviewer.

Here is information about the video:
Video type: [EXPLAINER / AD / TRAINING]
AI tools used: [E.G. HEYGEN FOR AVATAR, RUNWAY FOR B-ROLL, ELEVENLABS FOR VOICE]
Video length: [LENGTH]
Client industry: [INDUSTRY]

Give me a quality audit checklist covering:
1. Audio issues to listen for (AI voice artifacts, pacing problems, unnatural pauses)
2. Visual issues to look for (avatar lip-sync errors, unnatural blinking, background inconsistencies, text readability)
3. Brand alignment checks (does it match their colors, tone, and audience expectations)
4. Platform fit checks (correct aspect ratio, caption readiness, thumbnail potential)
5. Legal/compliance flags (any claims that could be misleading, any music or footage that needs licensing verification)
6. The 3 most common reasons clients reject AI videos and how to check for each before sending

Format as a numbered checklist I can print and use for every project.

commonMistakes.mistake: Skipping the script approval step and going straight into AI video production
commonMistakes.why: AI video tools like HeyGen and Synthesia are time-consuming to re-render. If a client hates the script after you've already produced the video, you're rebuilding from scratch — burning 3-5 hours on a job you already spent 3-5 hours on. Most operators underestimate how often clients change their minds once they see something visual.
commonMistakes.prevention: Build a mandatory script approval checkpoint into every contract. Client signs off on the written script (and optionally a storyboard) before a single frame is rendered. State explicitly in your proposal that post-production script changes incur a revision fee.

commonMistakes.mistake: Underpricing because you're comparing your rate to offshore video editors, not to the value delivered
commonMistakes.why: AI video production compresses production time dramatically — a video that took a traditional agency 3 weeks now takes you 3 days. Operators see this speed as a reason to charge less. Clients see the output (a professional video), not your process.
commonMistakes.prevention: Price based on the client's outcome and market rate for the deliverable, not your hours. Your AI efficiency is your margin, not your discount.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using AI-generated stock footage or music without verifying licensing
commonMistakes.why: Tools like Runway and Pika generate visuals that may incorporate training data from copyrighted sources. Separately, many operators pull background music from YouTube libraries or free sites without reading the commercial use terms. If a client uses your video in paid advertising and gets a copyright claim or takedown, you are exposed — especially if your contract doesn't address IP.
commonMistakes.prevention: Use only explicitly commercially licensed music (Epidemic Sound, Artlist, or Pixabay commercial tier). For AI-generated video, use tools with clear commercial output licenses (Runway and Pika both offer commercial plans — read the terms). Add an IP indemnification clause to your client contract.

commonMistakes.mistake: Taking on every type of video project instead of specializing in one format or niche
commonMistakes.why: AI video production has a steep learning curve per tool and per format. Explainer videos, training videos, UGC-style ads, and avatar-based demos all require different tools, workflows, and client expectations. Trying to be a generalist while you're still learning means slow production, inconsistent quality, and no repeatable process — which means no scale.
commonMistakes.prevention: Pick one video format (e.g. 60-second explainer ads) and one client niche (e.g. SaaS companies or real estate agents) for your first 90 days. Get fast and good at that one thing. Expand only after you have a repeatable workflow that takes you under 8 hours per project.

commonMistakes.mistake: Delivering videos without a written contract or revision policy
commonMistakes.why: Clients who haven't signed anything feel entitled to unlimited changes, scope additions, and delayed payments. 'Can you just tweak the ending?' turns into a full re-edit. Without a contract, you have no legal footing to charge for extra work or enforce payment terms.
commonMistakes.prevention: Send it before any work starts — no exceptions.

Set up platform and recruit 10-15 founding members
Launch publicly with rituals and accountability pods

Add premium tiers and course/coaching upsells

audience.industry: Various — whoever shares your niche expertise
painPoints: Building alone with no one to bounce ideas off or get feedback from
Consuming content but not implementing because there is no accountability
Information overload — too many courses, not enough community and support
Impostor syndrome and lack of confidence because they have no peer group

firstCustomerTactics: Start a free community (Discord/Slack) to test the concept and build initial engagement before charging
Run a free 5-day challenge on your topic to build urgency and demonstrate your teaching style

Personally DM your 20 most engaged followers and offer them early access

phases.name: Foundation

tasks.title: Define your community positioning
tasks.description: Answer these questions: (1) Who is this community for? (3) Why will they pay YOU vs. consuming free content? (4) What can they get here they cannot get anywhere else? Write a one-paragraph manifesto that captures the community's soul.
tasks.deliverable: Community positioning document with manifesto, target member profile, and unique value proposition

tasks.title: Choose platform and set up community
tasks.description: Pick your platform based on your audience: Skool (gamification, simple), Circle (professional, courses), Discord (tech-savvy, free to host). Set up channels/spaces: Welcome, Introductions, Wins, Q&A, Resources, Off-Topic. Create community guidelines and a welcome flow that makes new members post within 24 hours.
tasks.deliverable: Community platform set up with channels, guidelines, and welcome flow

tasks.title: Create 30 days of seed content
tasks.description: Pre-load the community with valuable content so it does not feel empty when founding members join. Include: 5 resource posts (guides, templates, tools), 3 discussion prompts, 2 mini-tutorials, and your "Start Here" guide. Use AI to help draft, but add personal stories and examples.
tasks.deliverable: 30 days of scheduled content + Start Here guide

tasks.title: Recruit 10-15 founding members via DMs
tasks.description: Personally reach out to your most engaged followers, email subscribers, or colleagues. Frame it as: "I'm building something special and want you to be part of shaping it." Do NOT launch publicly until you have 10+ founding members — an empty community is a dead community.

phases.name: Launch
phases.description: Open publicly, establish culture, and hit 30 members

tasks.title: Host founding member kickoff call
tasks.description: Run a 60-minute live call with all founding members. Introduce yourself, have everyone share their #1 goal for the next 90 days, and explain the community roadmap. Record this — it becomes social proof. End with action: everyone posts their goal in the community before leaving the call.
tasks.deliverable: Kickoff call completed, recording available, all members active

tasks.title: Establish weekly rhythms
tasks.description: Set up recurring community rituals: Monday = Set Your Weekly Goal, Wednesday = Q&A Thread or Live Call, Friday = Win of the Week. These rhythms are the backbone of retention.
tasks.deliverable: Weekly rhythm documented and first 2 weeks executed

tasks.title: Launch publicly with urgency
tasks.description: Announce the community on all social channels. Use a waitlist or limited-spots model to create urgency. Share founding member testimonials (even if just screenshots of their intro posts). Run a free live workshop that funnels to a community pitch at the end. Email your full list with a 48-hour early-bird offer.
tasks.deliverable: Public launch executed, 15+ new member applications

tasks.title: Set up accountability pods
tasks.description: Group members into pods of 4-5 people with similar goals. Each pod checks in weekly (async or live). Facilitate the first pod meeting, then let them self-organize.
tasks.deliverable: Accountability pods formed and first check-ins completed

tasks.title: Create member referral engine
tasks.description: Launch a referral program: members get 1 month free for every new member they refer. Create a shareable "invite your friend" link. Give members social media templates they can use to share the community.

tasks.title: Host monthly guest expert sessions
tasks.description: Invite an expert your members admire for a 45-minute live Q&A. This is surprisingly easy — most experts say yes because it is free promotion for them. Record and add to your resource library. These sessions are the #1 reason members upgrade to higher tiers.

tasks.title: Create content flywheel

Generate a 10-minute YouTube script for a Top 10 list in [niche].

Niche: [niche]
Topic: [Top 10 X]

Structure:

HOOK (0-15s):

commonMistakes.mistake: Picking low-RPM niches (entertainment, gaming, comedy)
commonMistakes.prevention: Personal finance, tech reviews, business analysis, true crime are top tiers.

commonMistakes.mistake: AI voice that sounds robotic
commonMistakes.why: Early ElevenLabs voices + bad prosody = audiences click away in 10 seconds. Retention dies. Algorithm punishes.
commonMistakes.prevention: Use ElevenLabs v2+ voices (Adam, Rachel, Antoni). Add SSML pauses. Match voice to niche tone.

commonMistakes.mistake: Not using thumbnail A/B testing
commonMistakes.why: YouTube Studio includes free thumbnail A/B testing. Most creators ignore it. CTR is the #1 ranking factor.
commonMistakes.prevention: Test 2-3 thumbnails on every video. Pick winner after 48 hours.

commonMistakes.mistake: No watch-time hook in first 10s
commonMistakes.why: YouTube measures retention from second 0. Slow opens = audience leaves = no algo distribution.
commonMistakes.prevention: First 10 seconds: pattern interrupt + tease + value promise. Rewrite intros until first 10s retains 80%+.

commonMistakes.mistake: Going too long before niching
commonMistakes.why: YouTube needs to categorize you. Mixed-topic channels confuse algo for months.
commonMistakes.prevention: Lock niche in week 1. First 30 videos all same niche. Adjacent topics only after 1K subs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring YouTube Shorts as growth lever
commonMistakes.why: Skipping Shorts = slow ramp.
commonMistakes.prevention: Auto-clip every long-form into 3-5 Shorts (OpusClip). Daily Shorts drive subs faster.

commonMistakes.mistake: Music licensing violations
commonMistakes.why: YouTube auto-detects copyrighted music. Strikes accumulate → channel termination.
commonMistakes.prevention: NEVER use commercial music without license.
